Having seated him on a precious throne under the white parasol, the King made offerings with countless varieties of aquatic and terrestrial flowers and golden flowers. Surrounded by sixteen thousand dancing women adorned with all ornaments, he said: "Manifest to my eyes and those of these people the physical form of the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the possessor of infinite wisdom, who turned the noble Wheel of the True Dhamma." Then, the Buddha-form manifested by that Nāga king—adorned with the eighty minor marks and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man produced by the power of merit diffused throughout his entire body—was like the surface of water adorned with blooming red, blue, and white lotuses; like the expanse of the sky illuminated by the clear radiance of the host of stars; like the peak of a golden mountain surrounded by rainbows and lightning-streaks glowing with the evening light, beautiful with the circle of a fathom-long radiance interwoven with rays of various colors such as blue, yellow, and red; and beautiful with a lovely head glowing with a pure crest of various hues. Beholding this Buddha-form, which is the source of delight for the eyes of Brahmās, devas, humans, Nāgas, and Yakkhas, the King performed the "Eye-Worship" for seven days.

It is said that after his consecration, the King followed external sects for three years. In the fourth year, he gained faith in the Buddha's Dispensation. His father, King Bindusāra, had been a devotee of Brahmins; he had established daily alms for about sixty thousand Brahmins, Brahminical sects, and Pandaranga wanderers. King Asoka also continued the alms-giving established by his father within his palace. One day, while standing at the lion-window, he saw them eating with behavior devoid of tranquility, with unrestrained senses and undisciplined deportment. He thought: "It is proper to investigate such alms-giving and give only in a suitable place." Having thought thus, he said to his ministers: "Go, friends, to your own..."
34:
The King said, "Bring to the palace recluses and Brahmins who are considered virtuous; we shall give alms." The ministers replied, "Very well, O King," and having accepted the King's command, they brought various Pandaranga wanderers, Ājīvakas, Nigaṇṭhas, and others, saying, "Great King, these are our Arahants."

Then the King, having prepared high and low seats in the palace, said, "Let them come," and told those who arrived, "Venerable sirs, sit on seats appropriate for yourselves." Among them, some sat on small wicker chairs, and some sat on small wooden plank seats. Seeing them, the King knew, "There is no inner essence of virtue in these people," and after giving them suitable food and snacks, he sent them away.

As time passed in this way, one day the King, standing at the lion-window, saw the novice Nigrodha walking through the palace courtyard—tamed, guarded, with peaceful senses, and endowed with inspiring deportment. Who was this novice named Nigrodha? He was the son of Prince Sumana, the eldest son of King Bindusāra.

## In this matter, the chronological account is as follows:

While King Bindusāra was weak, Prince Asoka abandoned the kingship of Ujjeni which he had obtained, came and brought the entire city under his control, and captured Prince Sumana. On that very day, Prince Sumana's queen, named Sumanā, was heavily pregnant. She left the palace in disguise and, heading towards a certain Caṇḍāla village not far away, heard the voice of a deity dwelling in a banyan (Nigrodha) tree near the headman's house, saying, "Sumanā, come here." She went to the deity. The deity, by her own power, created a hall and gave it to her, saying, "Dwell here." She entered that hall. On the very day she arrived, she gave birth to a son. Because he was protected and taken care of by the banyan-tree deity, she named him "Nigrodha." From the day he saw her, the Caṇḍāla headman regarded her as his own master's daughter and constantly looked after her. The princess lived in that hall for seven years. Prince Nigrodha also reached the age of seven. At that time, an Arahant named Mahāvaruṇa, seeing the boy's potential for attaining the fruit of Arahantship, stayed near that Caṇḍāla village to protect him. Thinking, "The boy is now seven years old; it is time to ordain him," he informed the princess and ordained Prince Nigrodha.
35:
Thinking it was time for his ordination, the King informed the princess and had the youth Nigrodha ordained. At the very end of the shaving of his hair, the youth attained the fruit of Arahantship. One day, early in the morning, after attending to his bodily needs and performing his duties toward his teacher and preceptor, the novice Nigrodha took his bowl and robes, thinking, 'I will go to the door of my mother, the lay devotee.' To reach his mother's residence, he had to enter the city through the southern gate, pass through the center of the city, and exit through the eastern gate.

At that time, King Asoka, the Righteous King, was walking to and fro on the palace balcony, facing the east. At that very moment, the novice Nigrodha arrived at the royal courtyard, with his senses calmed and his mind at peace, looking only a yoke's length ahead. Regarding this arrival, it is said: 'One day, while the King was standing at the palace window, he saw the novice Nigrodha walking across the royal courtyard—tamed, guarded, with senses calmed, and perfect in deportment.' Upon seeing the novice, the King thought: 'All these people have distracted minds and are like frightened deer. But this youth has an undistracted mind; his looking forward and aside, his bending and stretching, are exceedingly graceful. Surely, there must be the supramundane Dhamma within him.' As soon as the King saw him, faith arose in his heart and love was established. Why was that? It is said that in a previous life, when they were performing meritorious deeds, this novice was the King's elder brother, a merchant. For it has been said:

'By previous association, or by present benefit,
Thus is that love born, like a lotus in the water.'

Then the King, with a heart full of love and great respect, sent ministers, saying, 'Call that novice.' Thinking they were taking too long, he sent two or three more, saying, 'Let him come quickly.' The novice came in his natural, composed manner. Knowing a suitable seat, the King said, 'Please sit down.' The novice looked here and there and, reflecting, 'There are no other monks now,' approached the royal throne over which the white parasol was raised, and signaled to the King to take his bowl. Seeing the novice approaching the throne, the King thought: 'This very day, this novice will be the master of this house.' The novice handed his bowl to the King and, ascending the throne, sat down. The King offered all the...
36:
...congee, hard food, and special rice prepared for himself. The novice accepted only as much as was necessary for his sustenance. At the end of the meal, the King asked, 'Do you know the advice given by your Teacher?' 'I know it in part, Great King,' he replied. 'Dear child, preach it to me as well,' the King requested. 'Very well, Great King,' the novice replied, and for the sake of the King's appreciation, he preached the Appamāda-vagga (Chapter on Heedfulness) from the Dhammapada, which was suitable for a king.

As soon as the King heard the verse, 'Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness is the path to death,' he said, 'I understand, dear child; please conclude.' At the end of the talk, he said, 'Dear child, I give you eight permanent meals (niccabhatta).' The novice said, 'Great King, I give these to my preceptor (upajjhāya).' 'Dear child, who is this preceptor?' the King asked. 'Great King, he is the one who, seeing faults small and large, admonishes and reminds me.' 'Dear child, I give you another eight meals.' 'Great King, I give these to my teacher (ācariya).' 'Dear child, who is this teacher?' 'Great King, he is the one who establishes me in the Dhamma to be learned in this Dispensation.' 'Very well, dear child, I give you another eight meals.' 'Great King, I give these to the Saṅgha of monks.' 'Dear child, who is this Saṅgha of monks?' 'Great King, it is the Saṅgha depending on whom the ordination and higher ordination of my teacher, my preceptor, and myself occurred.' The King, with a heart exceedingly delighted, said again, 'Dear child, I give you another eight meals.' The novice accepted, saying, 'Very well.' On the following day, he took thirty-two monks, entered the inner palace, and had his meal. The King requested, 'Let another thirty-two monks receive alms with you tomorrow,' and by this means, increasing the number daily, he discontinued the meals for sixty thousand brahmins and wandering ascetics, and established permanent meals for sixty thousand monks in the inner palace, solely out of the faith he had in the Elder Nigrodha. The Elder Nigrodha also established the King and his retinue in the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, and transformed the King's faith from that of a worldling into unshakable faith in the Buddha's Dispensation. Furthermore, the King had a great monastery named Asokārāma built and established permanent meals for sixty thousand monks. Throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, in eighty-four thousand cities, he had eighty-four thousand monasteries built, adorned with eighty-four thousand stupas, through righteous means alone, and not unrighteously.

One day, it is said, the King, having given a great gift at the Asokārāma monastery, sat in the midst of sixty thousand monks. Having invited the Saṅgha with the four requisites, he asked this question: 'Venerable sirs, how extensive is the Dhamma preached by the Blessed One?' The Elder (Elder Moggaliputtatissa) replied, 'Great King, the Dhamma preached by the Blessed One has nine factors (navaṅgasatthusāsana) and consists of eighty-four thousand Dhamma-aggregates (dhammakkhandha).'
37:
(The King) asked, "Venerable sir, how extensive is the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One?" "Great King, the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One consists of nine limbs in terms of its parts, and eighty-four thousand units of Dhamma (dhammakkhandhas) in terms of its groups," the Elder replied.

The King, gaining faith in the Dhamma, thought, "I will honor each unit of Dhamma with a monastery." In a single day, he spent ninety-six crores of wealth and commanded his ministers, "Come, friends! Have one monastery built in each city, and thus have eighty-four thousand monasteries built in eighty-four thousand cities."

He himself began the work for the Asoka Mahāvihāra at Asokārāma. The Saṅgha appointed the Elder Indagutta, a possessor of great psychic power and majesty, an Arahant (khīṇāsava), as the supervisor of the new construction (navakammādhiṭṭhāyaka). Whatever work could not be completed, the Elder finished it through his own power. In this way, the construction of the monasteries was completed in three years. On the same day, messages arrived from all the cities.

The ministers informed the King, "Great King, the eighty-four thousand monasteries are now completed." The King had a drum beaten throughout the city, announcing, "Seven days from now, there will be a great festival for the monasteries (vihāramaha). Let all the people undertake the eight precepts and prepare the festival for the monasteries both inside and outside the city."

Then, after seven days had passed, the King, adorned with all ornaments and surrounded by a fourfold army numbering many hundreds of thousands, toured the city which was decorated and prepared by the enthusiastic multitude, appearing even more glorious than the celestial capital Amaravatī. He went to the monastery and stood in the midst of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.

At that moment, eighty crore monks and nine million six hundred thousand nuns had assembled. Among them, the Arahant monks alone numbered one hundred thousand. It occurred to those monks, "If the King sees his own extraordinary merit in its entirety, he will gain even greater faith in the Buddha's Dispensation (Sāsana)." Thereupon, they performed the miracle called the 'Opening of the World' (loka-vivaraṇa). While standing in Asokārāma, the King, looking in the four directions, saw the entire Jambudīpa bounded by the ocean, and the eighty-four thousand monasteries shining with the grand monastery festival offerings.

Seeing that splendor, the King was filled with sublime joy and rapture. Thinking, "Has such joy and rapture ever arisen in anyone else before?" he asked the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, "Venerable sirs, who has made a great sacrifice (mahāpariccāga) in the Dispensation of our Lord of the World, the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala)?"
38:
"Whose sacrifice is greatest?" (the King asked). The Bhikkhu Saṅgha entrusted the responsibility of answering to the Elder Moggaliputtatissa. The Elder said, "Great King, even during the lifetime of the Tathāgata, there was no donor of requisites (paccayadāyaka) like you; your sacrifice alone is indeed great."

When the King heard the Elder's words, his entire body was suffused with sublime joy and rapture, and he thought, "It is said that there was no donor of requisites like me even during the lifetime of the Buddha. It is said that my sacrifice is great. It is said that I am supporting the Dispensation with offerings. But even so, am I an heir (dāyāda) to the Dispensation, or am I not?" Then he asked the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, "Venerable sirs, am I an heir to the Dispensation?"

Then the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, hearing the King's words and perceiving the perfection of the supporting conditions (upanissaya) of Prince Mahinda (for attaining the paths and fruits), thought, "If this prince ordains, the Dispensation will flourish greatly." He then said to the King, "Great King, by such a sacrifice one does not yet become an heir to the Dispensation; rather, one is merely reckoned as a 'donor of requisites' or a 'supporter' (upaṭṭhāka). Great King, even if one were to give a heap of requisites reaching from the earth to the Brahma world, such a person is still not reckoned as an 'heir to the Dispensation'."

"Then how, venerable sir, does one become an heir to the Dispensation?" the King asked. "Great King, whether one is wealthy or poor, if one lets one's own dear son or daughter ordain in the Dispensation, such a person, Great King, is called an heir to the Dispensation."

When this was said, King Asoka thought, "It is said that although I have made such a sacrifice, I have not yet attained the status of an heir to the Dispensation." Desiring to become an heir to the Dispensation, he looked here and there and saw Prince Mahinda standing nearby. Seeing him, it occurred to the King, "Although I have wished to appoint this prince to the position of Crown Prince (uparāja) since the time Prince Tissa ordained, yet ordination is superior even to the position of Crown Prince." Then he said to the prince, "Dear son, can you ordain?"

The prince, who had already desired to ordain since the time Prince Tissa ordained, became exceedingly joyful upon hearing the King's words and said, "Great King, I will ordain. By letting me ordain, may you become an heir to the Dispensation."

At that time, Princess Saṅghamittā was also standing in that same place. Her husband, Prince Aggibrahmā, had already ordained along with the Crown Prince Tissa. When the King saw Saṅghamittā, he asked, "Dear daughter, can you also ordain?" She replied, "Great King, it is well; I too can ordain." Knowing the intention of his son and daughter, the King, with a joyful mind, said to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, "Venerable sirs, please ordain this youth and maiden, and make me an heir to the Dispensation."
39:
(Aggibrahmā, the husband of Saṅghamittā,) had already ordained along with Tissakumāra. Seeing Saṅghamittā, the King said, "Dear daughter, will you also be able to ordain?" She replied, "Yes, dear father, I am able." Having obtained the consent of his son and daughter, the King, with a joyful heart, said to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, "Venerable Sirs, please ordain these children and make me an heir to the Sāsana." Accepting the King's request, the Saṅgha ordained Prince Mahinda with Moggaliputtatissa Thera as his preceptor (upajjhāya) and Mahādeva Thera as his teacher (ācariya). He was given higher ordination with Majjhantika Thera as his teacher. At that time, the Prince had just completed twenty years of age. Right within that ordination hall (sīmā), Prince Mahinda attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). For Princess Saṅghamittā, the teacher was Āyupālittherī and the preceptor was Dhammapālittherī. At that time, Saṅghamittā was eighteen years old. Immediately after her ordination, she was established in the training (sikkhā) within that same ordination hall. At the time of their ordination, the King had been consecrated for six years.

Thereafter, from the time of his higher ordination, Mahinda Thera studied the Dhamma and Vinaya under his own preceptor. Within three years, he mastered the entire Theravāda Tipiṭaka along with the commentaries as recited in the two councils, and became the leader of a thousand monks who were pupils of his preceptor. At that time, the Righteous King Asoka had been consecrated for nine years. In the eighth year of the King's consecration, Kontaputtatissa Thera, while wandering for alms to treat an illness, did not receive even a measure of ghee. Due to the severity of the illness, his life-force was exhausted. After exhorting the Bhikkhu Saṅgha to be diligent, he sat cross-legged in the air, entered the fire element (tejodhātu), and attained Parinibbāna. When the King heard of this, he performed honors for the Thera and thought, "While I am reigning, the four requisites are so difficult for the monks to obtain." He then had ponds constructed at the four gates of the city, filled them with medicines, and offered them.

At that time, the King's daily revenue was four hundred thousand coins from the four gates of Pāṭaliputta and one hundred thousand from the assembly hall, totaling five hundred thousand daily. From this, the King gave one hundred thousand daily to Nigrodha Thera. He also gave one hundred thousand for offerings of incense and flowers at the Buddha's shrine (cetiya).
40:
One hundred thousand was given for the Dhamma, to provide the four requisites for the learned monks and those who bear the Dhamma (dhammadhara). One hundred thousand was for the Saṅgha, and one hundred thousand for medicines at the four gates. Thus, great gain and honor arose within the Sāsana. The heretics (titthiyas), deprived of gain and honor to the point of not even obtaining food and clothing, desired gain and honor and ordained themselves in the Sāsana. They presented their own views, saying, "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya." Even those who did not receive ordination shaved their heads themselves, wore saffron robes, and wandered through the monasteries, joining the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, Saṅgha acts (saṅghakamma), and group acts (gaṇakamma). The monks would not perform the Uposatha with them. Then, Moggaliputtatissa Thera reflected, "Now this dispute (adhikaraṇa) has arisen; before long it will become severe. It is not possible to settle this while living in the midst of these monks." Entrusting his group to Mahinda Thera and wishing to live in comfort, he went to Ahogaṅga Mountain.

Those heretics, even when rebuked by the Bhikkhu Saṅgha according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher's instruction, did not abide by the practice consistent with the Dhamma and Vinaya. They stirred up various troubles, stains, and thorns for the Sāsana. Some worshipped fire, some tormented themselves with the fivefold heat-asceticism (pañcātapa), some followed the course of the sun, and some proclaimed, "We will destroy your Dhamma and Vinaya." At that time, the Bhikkhu Saṅgha no longer performed the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā with those heretics. For seven years, the Uposatha was suspended at Asokārāma monastery. This matter was reported to the King. The King commanded a minister, "Go to the monastery, settle the dispute, and have the Uposatha performed."

That minister, not daring to question the King further, approached other ministers and said, "The King has sent me, saying, 'Go to the monastery, settle the dispute, and have the Uposatha performed.' How can the dispute be settled?" They replied, "We think that just as rebels are killed when suppressing border conflicts, the King likely wishes to kill those monks who do not perform the Uposatha." Then, that minister went to the monastery, convened the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, and said, "I have been sent by the King to have the Uposatha performed. Venerable Sirs, perform the Uposatha now." The monks replied, "We do not perform the Uposatha with heretics." Then, the minister began to behead the monks with a sword, starting from the seat of the senior elders.
41:
Elder Tissa saw the minister’s perverted behavior. Elder Tissa was no ordinary person; he was Prince Tissa, the King’s younger brother born of the same mother. After his consecration, the King had appointed the prince to the position of viceroy. One day, while wandering in the forest, the prince saw a large herd of deer playing joyfully. Seeing this, he thought: "Even these grass-eating deer play like this; why then should these recluses, who eat choice food from the royal palace and sleep on soft beds, not play?" Returning from the forest, he reported his thought to the King. The King thought, "The prince has developed a doubt in an improper place; now, I will make him understand." One day, pretending to be angry for some reason, he threatened him with the fear of death, saying, "Come, accept the kingship for seven days; after that, I shall kill you," and thus made him realize the matter. Thinking, "He will kill me on the seventh day," the prince could not bathe, eat, or sleep as he wished, and his body became extremely haggard and thin. Then the King asked him, "Why have you become like this?" "Because of the fear of death, O King," he replied. "Hey, Prince, even when you see a fixed death, you cannot be at ease or play? How then can the monks, who behold death bound to every inhalation and exhalation, play?" From then on, the prince gained faith in the Dispensation.

Another day, while going out to the forest to hunt and wandering about, he saw the Elder Yonaka Mahādhammarakkhita sitting while being fanned with a sal branch by a great elephant. Seeing this, he was filled with joy and thought, "When shall I too ordain like this Great Elder? Could that day ever come?" The Elder, knowing his intention, flew into the air while the prince was watching, stood on the surface of the water in the pond at Asokārāma, hung his robes in the air, and began to bathe.

Seeing the Elder's psychic power, the prince was greatly inspired and returned, saying, "I will ordain this very day," and informed the King, "O King, I shall ordain." Although the King pleaded in many ways, he could not prevent him. He had the road to Asokārāma decorated, made the prince wear festive attire, and escorted him to the monastery surrounded by an army. Hearing that the viceroy was to ordain, many monks prepared bowls and robes. The prince went to the Padhānaghara (meditation house) with a hundred thousand men and ordained under Elder Mahādhammarakkhita. The number of those who followed the prince into ordination was immeasurable. The prince ordained in the fourth year after the King's consecration. At that time, there was also a prince named Aggibrahmā, the King's nephew and the husband of Saṅghamittā. Saṅghamittā had already given birth to a son by that prince.
42:
The prince went to the Padhānaghara, the meditation house, with a hundred thousand men and ordained in the presence of Elder Mahādhammarakkhita himself. There was no limit to the number of people who followed the prince into ordination. The prince ordained in the fourth year after the King's consecration.

At that time, there was also another prince named Aggibrahmā, the King's nephew and the husband of Saṅghamittā. Saṅghamittā had given birth to only one son by that prince. Hearing that the viceroy had ordained, Prince Aggibrahmā also approached the King and requested, "Great King, I too shall ordain." The King consented, saying, "Ordain, dear son," and he ordained on that very day.

Thus, the King's younger brother, who received ordination followed by royalty of great wealth, should be known as Elder Tissa.

When Elder Tissa saw the minister acting so perversely, he thought, "The King would not send someone to kill the Elders; surely this must be the wrong grasp of this minister alone." He went and sat on a seat near the minister. Recognizing the Elder, the minister did not dare to strike him with his sword. He went to the King and reported, "Great King, I have cut off the heads of this many monks who did not wish to perform the Uposatha; now it is the turn of the Venerable Elder Tissa. What shall I do?"

As soon as the King heard this, he said, "Hey, minister! Did I send you to kill the monks?" Immediately, a burning sensation arose within his body. He went to the monastery and asked the Elders, "Venerable sirs, this minister did this without my command. In whom does this evil deed reside?" Some Elders said, "This was done because of your word; this evil belongs to you." Some said, "This evil belongs to both of you." Others asked, "Great King, did you have the intention, 'Let this man go and kill the monks'?"

"Venerable sirs, I had no such intention. I sent him with the wholesome intention, 'Let the community of monks perform the Uposatha in harmony,'" he replied. "If you sent him with a wholesome intention, there is no evil for you; this evil belongs only to the minister," they declared. The King became double-minded with doubt and asked, "Venerable sirs, is there any monk capable of cutting off this doubt of mine and supporting the Dispensation?" "Great King, there is the Elder named Moggaliputtatissa; he is capable of cutting off this doubt of yours and supporting the Dispensation," they replied.

On that very day, the King sent four Dhamma-preachers, each surrounded by a thousand monks, and four ministers, each surrounded by a thousand men, saying, "Go and bring the Elder." They went and said, "The King summons you." The Elder...
43:
The Elder did not come. For the second time, the King sent eight Dhamma preachers and eight ministers, each with a retinue of one thousand. He sent them with the instruction: "Go and bring the Elder, saying, 'Venerable Sir, the King invites you.'" They spoke as instructed. For the second time, the Elder did not come. The King asked the monks, "Venerable Sirs, I have sent for him twice; why does the Elder not come?"

"Great King, the Elder does not come because he was told, 'The King invites you.' However, if he is told, 'Venerable Sir, the Sāsana is declining; please be our helper to uphold the Sāsana,' then he will come."

Thereupon, the King gave instructions accordingly and sent sixteen Dhamma preachers and sixteen ministers, each with a retinue of one thousand. He further asked the monks, "Venerable Sir, is the Elder old or is he young?" "Great King, the Elder is very old," they replied. "Venerable Sir, will the Elder ride in a cart or a palanquin?" "Great King, he will not," they replied. "Venerable Sir, where does the Elder live?" "Great King, he lives upriver on the Gangā," they replied. The King said, "In that case, friends, tie boats together, seat the Elder upon them, arrange for guards on both banks of the river, and bring the Elder here."

The monks and ministers went to the Elder and delivered the King's message. When the Elder heard it, he reflected, "I ordained with the very purpose of upholding the Sāsana from the beginning. Now, that time has arrived for me." He then took his leather mat and arose. At that time, during the night, the King had a dream: "The Elder will arrive at Pāṭaliputta tomorrow." The dream was as follows: A noble elephant, entirely white, came and stroked the King from his head downwards and then held his right hand. The next day, the King asked the dream interpreters, "I have seen such a dream; what will happen to me?" One interpreter replied, "Great King, a noble ascetic (Samaṇanāga) will hold your right hand."

Then, as soon as the King heard that the Elder had arrived, he went to the bank of the Gangā, entered the river into knee-deep water to welcome him, and offered his hand to the Elder as he was descending from the boat. The Elder took the King's right hand. Seeing this, the sword-bearers, thinking, "We shall cut off the Elder's head," drew their swords from their scabbards. Why? For it is said that such is the custom among royal families: "The head of anyone who takes the King's hand must be cut off with a sword." The King, seeing only the shadow, said, "Previously, I found no peace because of my wrongdoings toward monks; do not offend the Elder." As for why the Elder [held] the King's...
44:
...held the hand: because he was invited by the King to answer questions, he held the hand thinking, "This King is my pupil (antevāsika)."

The King led the Elder to his garden, arranged for triple guards around the exterior, and having personally washed the Elder's feet and anointed them with oil, he sat near the Elder. Then, wishing to test him, thinking, "Is the Elder capable of cutting through my doubts, settling the arising dispute (adhikaraṇa), and upholding the Sāsana?", he said, "Venerable Sir, I wish to see a miracle (pāṭihāriya)." "Great King, what kind of miracle do you wish to see?" "Venerable Sir, I wish to see an earthquake." "Great King, do you wish to see the whole earth shake, or a partial earthquake?" "Venerable Sir, of these two, which is more difficult?" "Great King, in a bronze bowl full of water, is it more difficult to shake all the water, or only half of it?" "Venerable Sir, shaking only half is more difficult." "Great King, even so, causing a partial earthquake is much more difficult."

"Venerable Sir, in that case, I wish to see a partial earthquake." "Great King, if so, let a chariot be placed on the eastern side of an area one yojana in circumference, treading on the boundary with one wheel; let a horse be placed on the southern side, treading on the boundary with two legs; let a man be placed on the western side, treading on the boundary with one foot; and let a water bowl be placed on the northern side, treading on the boundary with half of its part." The King had it done accordingly. The Elder entered the Fourth Jhāna, which is the basis for higher knowledge (abhiññā), and after emerging, he resolved, "Let the King see," and made the determination to shake the earth for the extent of one yojana. On the eastern side, only the wheel of the chariot within the boundary shook; the other did not. Likewise, on the southern and western sides, only the legs of the horse and the man within the boundary shook, as did half of their bodies. On the northern side, only the half of the water that was within the boundary in the bowl shook; the rest remained still.

When the King saw that miracle, he reached the conclusion, "Now the Elder will be able to uphold the Sāsana," and he asked about his own remorse (kukkuccha): "Venerable Sir, I sent a minister to the monastery, saying, 'Go to the monastery, settle the dispute, and have the Uposatha performed.' That minister went to the monastery and killed this many monks. To whom does that evil (pāpa) belong?"

"Great King, did you have the intention, 'Let this minister go to the monastery and kill the monks'?" "No, Venerable Sir." "Great King, if you did not have such an intention, there is no evil for you." Then the Elder made the King understand this meaning by quoting this Sutta: "Monks, I say that intention (cetanā) is kamma. Having intended, one performs kamma through body, speech, and mind."
45:
The Elder made the King understand by means of this sutta: "Monks, I say that intention is kamma. Having intended, one performs kamma through body, speech, and mind." To further clarify this meaning, he cited the Tittira Jātaka: "O Great King, in the past, a partridge asked an ascetic: 'Many birds come here thinking that their kinsman is sitting here. Does the kamma of taking life (pāṇātipāta) affect me because of this? My mind is in doubt regarding this evil.' The ascetic asked: 'Do you have the intention that these birds, which come because they hear your voice and see your form, should be caught or killed?' 'No, venerable sir,' replied the partridge. Then the ascetic made him understand: 'If you have no such intention, there is no evil. Indeed, evil affects only the one who intends, not the one who does not intend.' He further said: 'If the mind does not offend, the kamma performed because of it does not affect one. Evil does not smear or cling to the virtuous person who has no concern for doing evil.'"

After the Elder had thus made the King understand, he resided in the royal garden for seven days and taught the King all the doctrines (samaya). On the seventh day, the King had the community of monks (Bhikkhu Saṅgha) assemble at Asokārāma. Having had screens set up and sitting within those screens, he grouped the monks of like views together. He then called each group of monks and asked: "What was the doctrine of the Fully Enlightened One?" Then the Eternalists (Sassatavādī) replied: "He was an Eternalist." Some Eternalists... and so on... the Finite-and-Infinite-ists (Antānantika), the Eel-wrigglers (Amarāvikkhepika), the Fortuitous-originationists (Adhiccasamuppannika), the Percipient-ists (Saññīvāda), the Non-percipient-ists (Asaññīvāda), the Neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient-ists (Nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda), the Annihilationists (Ucchedavāda), and the Nibbāna-in-this-life-ists (Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda) each replied: "He was a Nibbāna-in-this-life-ist."

Because the King had previously studied the doctrines, he realized, "These are not monks; they are external heretics (titthiya)." He gave them white clothes and disrobed them. All of them numbered sixty thousand. Then he called the other monks and asked: "Venerable sirs, what was the doctrine of the Fully Enlightened One?" "Great King, He was an Analyst (Vibhajjavādī)," they replied. When they said this, the King asked the Elder: "Venerable sir, was the Fully Enlightened One an Analyst?" "Yes, Great King," the Elder replied. Then the King said: "Venerable sir, the Dispensation (Sāsana) is now pure; let the Bhikkhu Saṅgha perform the Uposatha." Having provided protection, he entered the city.
46:
The unified Saṅgha assembled in harmony and performed the Uposatha. In that assembly, there were six million monks. In that gathering, Moggaliputtatissa Thera, crushing the doctrines of others, expounded the Kathāvatthu treatise. Then, selecting from among the six million monks, he took one thousand monks who were bearers of the Tipitaka, possessed of the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), and endowed with special qualities such as the three knowledges (tevijjā). Just as the Elder Mahākassapa and the Elder Yasa, son of Kākaṇḍaka, had chanted the Dhamma and Vinaya, he likewise chanted the Dhamma and Vinaya, cleansing all the stains of the Dispensation, and conducted the Third Council (Tatiya Saṅgīti). At the conclusion of the Council, the earth quaked in various ways. This Council was completed in nine months.

In the world—
Because it was performed by a thousand monks, it is called "Sahassikā";
And following the previous two, it is called the "Third Council" (Tatiya Saṅgīti).
This is the Third Council.

To this extent, regarding the question "Who brought it?", we have said: "In Jambudīpa, it was brought by a lineage of teachers starting from the Elder Upāli until the Third Council." The meaning of that statement has been clearly shown. Those teachers in the lineage are:
"Upāli, Dāsaka, Soṇaka, Siggava, and Tissa Moggaliputtatissa—these five victors,
Brought the Vinaya in the island named the glorious Jambu (Jambudīpa),
In an unbroken lineage until the Third Council."

After the Third Council, however, it was brought to this island (Sri Lanka) by Mahinda and others. Having learned it from the Elder Mahinda, it was brought for a time by the Elder Ariṭṭha and others. From then until today, it should be understood that it has been brought by the lineage of teachers who are the successive disciples of those Elders. As the ancient teachers said:
"Then Mahinda, Ittiya, Uttiya, Sambala,
And the wise Bhaddanāma (came here).
These Nagas (noble beings) of great wisdom came here from Jambudīpa;
They taught the Vinaya Piṭaka in Tambapaṇṇi."
47:
(These elders) taught the five Nikāyas and also the seven books of the Abhidhamma. After that, there were the wise Elder Ariṭṭha and the wise Elder Tissadatta.

There were the valiant Elder Kāḷasumana, the noble Elder named Dīgha, and the wise Elder Dīghasumana.

Again, there were the Elder Kāḷasumana, the Elder Nāga, the Elder Buddharakkhita, the wise Elder Tissa, and the wise Elder Deva.

Again, there were the wise Elder Sumana, who was valiant in the Vinaya, and the learned Elder Cūḷanāga, who was as difficult to overcome as a great elephant.

There were the Elder named Dhammapālita, who was worshipped by the virtuous in the Rohaṇa region, and his disciple, the greatly wise Elder named Khema, who was a bearer of the Three Piṭakas.

That Elder Khema shone brilliantly with wisdom on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, like the moon, the king of stars. There were also the wise Elder Upatissa and the Elder Phussadeva, who was a great speaker.

Again, there were the wise Elder Sumana, the learned Elder named Puppha, and the Elder Mahāsiva, who was skilled in all parts of the Piṭakas and was a great speaker.

Again, there were the wise Elder Upāli, who was valiant in the Vinaya, and the greatly wise Elder Mahānāga, who was skilled in the lineage of the True Dhamma.

Again, there were the wise Elder Abhaya, who was skilled in all parts of the Piṭakas, and the wise Elder Tissa, who was valiant in the Vinaya.

The disciple of that Elder Tissa, the greatly wise and learned Elder named Puppha, remained in Jambudīpa, protecting the Dispensation.

There were the wise Elder Cūḷābhaya, who was valiant in the Vinaya, and the wise Elder Tissa, who was skilled in the lineage of the True Dhamma.

There were the wise Elder Cūḷadeva, who was valiant in the Vinaya, and the wise Elder Siva, who was skilled in all parts of the Vinaya.

These noble elders, who possessed great wisdom, were experts in the Vinaya, and were skilled in the Path, illuminated the Vinaya Piṭaka on the island of Tambapaṇṇi.
48:
The following is the chronological account: It is said that after the Elder Moggaliputtatissa had conducted this Third Council, he reflected, "Where will the Dispensation be well-established in the future?" While reflecting thus, he perceived, "It will be well-established in the outlying border regions." That Elder assigned responsibilities to various monks and sent them to those respective regions. He sent the Elder Majjhantika to the Kasmīra-Gandhāra region, saying, "Go to this region and establish the Dispensation there." Having spoken in the same manner, he sent the Elder Mahādeva to the Mahiṃsaka region. He sent the Elder Rakkhita to the Vanavāsī region; the Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita to the Aparantaka region; the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita to the Mahāraṭṭha region; the Elder Mahārakkhita to the Yonaka world; the Elder Majjhima to the Himavanta region; and the Elders Soṇa and Uttara to Suvaṇṇabhūmi. He sent his own resident disciple, the Elder Mahinda, together with the Elders Ittiya, Uttiya, Sambala, and Bhaddasāla to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, saying, "Go to the island of Tambapaṇṇi and establish the Dispensation there." All of them, while going to their respective directions, went in groups of five, considering that "In the outlying border regions, a group of five monks is sufficient for the Upasampada ceremony."

At that time, in the Kasmīra-Gandhāra region, when the crops were ripening, a Naga King named Aravāဠa caused a hailstorm to fall, destroying the crops and washing them into the great ocean. The Elder Majjhantika, however, rose into the air from Pāṭaliputta and descended above the Aravāဠa Lake in the Himavanta, where he walked, stood, sat, and lay down upon the surface of the Aravāဠa Lake. When the young Nagas saw him, they reported to the Naga King Aravāဠa, "Great King, a man with a shaven head, wearing dyed robes made of torn pieces, is polluting our water." Immediately overcome with anger, the Naga King came out and, upon seeing the Elder, could not tolerate the sight and created various terrifying visions in the sky. Violent winds blew from all directions, trees were broken, mountain peaks fell, clouds thundered, lightning flashed, and thunderbolts struck; rain poured down as if the sky itself were splitting apart. Young Nagas of terrifying appearance gathered. The Naga King himself emitted smoke and flames and unleashed a rain of weapons. He threatened the Elder with harsh words such as, "Who is this shaven-headed man wearing robes made of torn pieces?" "Come, seize this man..."
49:
He commanded the Naga hosts, "Kill this ascetic, drive him out!" The Elder, having warded off all those terrifying sights with his own psychic power, spoke thus to the Naga King:

"Even if the entire world together with the devas were to come and threaten me, they would not be able to cause me fear or terror."

"O Great Naga, even if you were to lift up the entire earth, together with the oceans and mountains, and hurl it upon me,"

"even then, you would not be able to cause me fear or terror. On the contrary, O Lord of Serpents, it would only be your own destruction."

When he had spoken thus, the Naga King, his power broken and his efforts in vain, became miserable and dejected. The Elder, having shown him the Dhamma with a discourse suitable for that moment, having encouraged, inspired, and gladdened him, established him in the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, along with eighty-four thousand Nagas. Many other Yakkhas, Gandhabbas, and Kumbhaṇḍas living in the Himālaya also heard the Elder's Dhamma discourse and were established in the Refuges and Precepts. The Yakkha named Pañcaka, together with his wife the Yakkhinī and five hundred sons, was established in the first fruit (the fruit of Stream-entry). Then the Venerable Majjhantika Thera addressed all the Nagas, Yakkhas, and Rakkhasas, saying:

"From now on, do not give rise to anger as before. Living beings desire happiness; therefore, do not destroy the crops."

"Cultivate loving-kindness towards all beings; let humans live in peace."

They all consented to the Elder's words, saying, "Very well, Bhante," and followed his instructions. That very day was the time for the Naga King's festival of worship. Then the Naga King had his jewel-encrusted throne brought and prepared for the Elder. The Elder sat upon the throne. The Naga King stood nearby, fanning the Elder. At that moment, the inhabitants of the Kasmīra-Gandhāra region arrived and, seeing the Elder, thought, "The Elder is even more powerful than our Naga King," and they sat down after paying homage only to the Elder. The Elder preached the Āsīvisopama Sutta to them.
50:
(The Venerable Majjhantika) preached the Āsīvisopama Sutta. At the conclusion of the Sutta, eighty thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma, and a hundred thousand families went forth into the homeless life. From that time until today, the regions of Kasmīra and Gandhāra have been radiant with saffron robes and permeated by the scent of the monks' presence.

Having gone to Kasmīra-Gandhāra at that time,
The sage Majjhantika,
Having converted the wicked Naga,
Released many beings from their bonds.

The Elder Mahādeva also went to the Mahisakamandala region and preached the Devadūta Sutta. At the conclusion of the Sutta, forty thousand beings obtained the Eye of Dhamma, and forty thousand beings went forth.

The powerful Mahādeva, having gone to the Mahisa country,
And stirred them with the Devadūtas,
Released many beings from their bonds.

The Elder Rakkhita also went to the Vanavāsī country and, standing in the air, converted the inhabitants of Vanavāsī with the Anamatagga-pariyāya discourse. At the conclusion of that discourse, sixty thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma. About seventy thousand beings went forth, and five hundred monasteries were established. Thus, the Elder established the Dispensation in that country.

The powerful Elder Rakkhita, having gone to Vanavāsī,
And standing there in the sky,
Preached the Anamatagga discourse.

The Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita also went to the Aparanta country and, having converted the inhabitants of Aparanta by preaching the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta, he made seventy thousand beings drink the nectar of the Dhamma. From the Khattiya caste alone, one thousand men went forth, and more than six thousand women also went forth. Thus, the Elder established the Dispensation in that country.

Having entered Aparanta, Yonaka Dhammarakkhita,
Converted many people there,
With the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta.

The Elder Mahādhammarakkhita also went to the Mahāraṭṭha country and, having converted the inhabitants of Mahāraṭṭha by preaching the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka, he established eighty-four thousand beings in the paths and fruits. Thirteen thousand beings went forth. Thus, the Elder established the Dispensation in that country.

The sage Mahādhammarakkhita, having gone to Mahāraṭṭha,
And preached the Jātaka,
Converted a great multitude of people.
51:
The Elder Mahārakkhita also went to the Yonaka country and, having inspired the Yonaka world with the discourse on the Kāḷakārāma Sutta, bestowed the adornment of the Paths and Fruits upon more than one hundred and seventy thousand beings. Ten thousand people received ordination in the presence of that Elder. In this way, he too established the Dispensation there.

At that time, the sage (Elder) Mahārakkhita went to the Yonaka country,
And with the Kāḷakārāma Sutta, he inspired those Yonaka people.

The Elder Majjhima, however, went to the Himavanta region together with the Elder Kassapagotta, the Elder Aḷakadeva, the Elder Dundubhissara, and the Elder Mahādeva. Having inspired that region with the discourse on the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, he enabled eighty koṭis (eight hundred million) of beings to attain the treasures of the Paths and Fruits. The five Elders also inspired five countries. Approximately one hundred thousand people received ordination in the presence of each Elder. In this way, those Elders established the Dispensation there.

Having gone to the Himavanta, the Elder Majjhima inspired it,
While manifesting to the army of Yakkhas the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta.

The Elder Soṇa also went to Suvaṇṇabhūmi together with the Elder Uttara. At that time, a female ogre (rakkhasī) in that region used to emerge from the ocean and devour every child born in the royal palace. On that very day, a child was born in the royal palace. When the people saw the Elders, they thought, "These are companions of the ogres," and they came with weapons, intending to strike the Elders. The Elder asked, "Why do you come with weapons in your hands?" They replied, "Ogres devour every child born in the royal palace; you are companions of those ogres." The Elder said, "We are not companions of ogres. We are recluses (samaṇas) who abstain from taking life... (and so on) ...who abstain from drinking intoxicants, who eat only one meal a day, who are virtuous, and who possess good Dhamma." At that very moment, that female ogre emerged from the ocean with her followers, thinking, "A child is born in the royal palace; I will devour it." When the people saw that female ogre, they cried out in fear, "Venerable sirs, that female ogre is coming!" The Elder created illusory forms twice as large as the ogres and, with those forms, surrounded that female ogre and her followers in the middle, from both sides...
52:
...and encircled them. To that female ogre and her followers, this thought occurred: "Surely these [beings] have obtained this place (from King Vessavaṇa); we, however, shall become their food." Having thought thus, all the ogres fled in great terror and speed. The Elder also drove those ogres away until they were out of sight and established protection around the island (so they could not return). At that time, he inspired the great multitude of people who had assembled by preaching the Brahmajāla Sutta and established them in the Three Refuges and the Precepts. In that assembly, sixty thousand people attained the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya). Three thousand five hundred sons of good families received ordination, and one thousand five hundred daughters of good families also received ordination. In this way, the Elder Soṇa established the Dispensation there in Suvaṇṇabhūmi. From the time that protection was established, they named the children born in the royal palace only by the name 'Soṇuttara'.

Having gone to Suvaṇṇabhūmi, Soṇa and Uttara of great psychic power,
After driving away the spirits (pisācas), preached the Brahmajāla Sutta.

The Elder Mahinda, having been requested by his preceptor (upajjhāya) and the Saṅgha of monks, "Go to the island of Tambapaṇṇi and establish the Dispensation," reflected: "Is it now the time for me to go to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, or is it not yet the time?" Then, as he investigated, the thought occurred to him: "It is not yet the time." Why did this occur to him upon seeing what? It was because he saw the aged state of King Muṭasiva. Furthermore, he thought: "This king is very old; it is not possible to support and uplift the Dispensation by relying on him. But now, his son Devānampiyatissa will rule. It will be possible to support and uplift the Dispensation by relying on him. Well then, until that time arrives, I shall visit my relatives. Whether we shall return to this region again or not (let us go for now)."

Having thought thus, the Elder Mahinda paid homage to his preceptor and the Saṅgha of monks and departed from the Asokārāma monastery. Together with the four Elders, Iṭṭhiya and the others, the novice Sumana (son of Saṅghamittā), and the lay devotee named Bhaṇḍuka, he wandered for alms in the Dakkhiṇāgiri region around the city of Rājagaha, spending six months while visiting his relatives. Then, in due course, he arrived at the city named Vedisa, the residence of his mother. It is said that when King Asoka was a prince and had obtained the province, while going to Ujjeni, he reached the city of Vedisa and took the daughter of the merchant of Vedisa. On that very day, she conceived and gave birth to Prince Mahinda in Ujjeni. When the prince was fourteen years old, the King received his consecration. That mother of the prince...
53:
At that time, the mother was living in the house of her relatives. Therefore, it is said: "Furthermore, in due course, he arrived at the city of Vedisanagara, where his mother's residence was located."

Upon seeing the Elder who had arrived, the Queen, who was the Elder's mother, paid homage by placing her head at his feet, offered alms-food, and then invited the Elder to the Vedisagiri Mahāvihāra monastery, which she herself had built. While the Elder was staying in that monastery, he thought: "Our task here is finished; is it now the time to go to the island of Laṅkā?" Then he thought: "Let King Devānampiyatissa first enjoy the consecration sent by my father; let him also hear of the virtues of the Triple Gem; and let him go out from the city for a festival and ascend Missaka Mountain; then I shall see him there."

After that, he stayed in that very monastery for another full month. When the month had passed and the Uposatha day of the full moon of the month of Jeṭṭhamūla arrived, all the Elders consulted together: "Is it now the time for us to go to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, or is it not yet time?" Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"At that time, there was the Elder of the Saṅgha named Mahinda;
There were also the Elders Iṭṭhiya, Uttiya, Bhaddasāla, and Sambala.
There was also the novice Sumana, of great psychic power and possessed of the six higher knowledges.
Bhaṇḍuka Upāsaka, who had seen the Four Noble Truths, was the seventh among them.
Thus, these great noble ones consulted together in private."

Then Sakka, the lord of devas, approached Venerable Mahinda and said: "Venerable sir, King Muṭasiva has passed away; now King Devānampiyatissa is reigning. The Fully Enlightened Buddha also prophesied of you: 'In the future, a monk named Mahinda will bring faith to the island of Tambapaṇṇi.' Therefore, venerable sir, it is time for you to go to that excellent island; I too shall be your companion."

Why did Sakka speak thus? It is said that the Blessed One, while at the foot of the Bodhi tree, surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye and, seeing the future prosperity of this island, spoke of this matter and commanded: "At that time, you too should be a companion." That is why he spoke thus. The Elder accepted his words and, together with the other six including himself, flew into the air from Vedisaka Mountain and landed on Missaka Mountain to the east of the city of Anurādhapura. That mountain is now also known as 'Cetiyapabbata.' Therefore, the ancient teachers said:
54:
"Having stayed for thirty nights in the royal monastery on Vedisagiri Mountain, they consulted: 'It is time for our journey; let us go to the excellent island.'

Those Elders flew up from Jambudīpa into the sky like king swans and descended upon the excellent mountain.

In front of the best of cities, on the mountain resembling a dark cloud, they landed on Sīlakūṭa (the stone peak), like swans on a mountain top."

Thus, it should be understood that Venerable Mahinda Thera, arriving with Iṭṭhiya and the others, established the Sāsana in this island of Laṅkā in the 236th year after the Parinibbāna of the Fully Enlightened Buddha.

Indeed, the Fully Enlightened Buddha attained Parinibbāna in the eighth year of King Ajātasattu. In that very year, Prince Vijaya, the son of Prince Sīhabāhu and the first king of the island of Tambapaṇṇi, came to this island and established human settlement. In the fourteenth year of King Udayabhadda in Jambudīpa, King Vijaya passed away here (after reigning for 38 years). In the fifteenth year of King Udayabhadda, a prince named Paṇḍuvāsudeva became king in this island. In the twentieth year of King Nāgadāsaka in that land, King Paṇḍuvāsudeva passed away here (after reigning for 30 years). In that same year, a prince named Abhaya became king in this island. In the seventeenth year of King Susunāga in that land, twenty years of King Abhaya's reign were completed here. Then, in the twentieth year of Abhaya, a rebel (dāmarika) named Paṇḍukābhaya seized the kingship. In the sixteenth year of King Kālāśoka in that land, seventeen years of King Paṇḍukābhaya were completed here. Those years, together with the one year (of interregnum) mentioned below, make eighteen years. In the fourteenth year of King Candagutta in that land, King Paṇḍukābhaya passed away here (after reigning for 70 years). King Muṭasiva became king. In the seventeenth year of King Asokadhammarāja in that land, King Muṭasiva passed away here (after reigning for 60 years). King Devānampiyatissa became king.

After the Parinibbāna of the Fully Enlightened Buddha, King Ajātasattu reigned for twenty-four years, King Udayabhadda for sixteen years, Kings Anuruddha and Muṇḍa for eight years, King Nāgadāsaka for twenty-four years, King Susunāga for eighteen years, his son King Kālāśoka for twenty-eight years, and then his sons, the ten brother-kings, reigned for twenty-two years. After them, the nine Nandas reigned for twenty-two years, King Candagutta for twenty-four years, and King Bindusāra for twenty-eight years. At the end of that king's reign, King Asokadhammarāja became king. Four years passed before his consecration. In the eighteenth year after his consecration, Venerable Mahinda Thera established the Sāsana in this island.
55:
Asoka attained kingship. Four years passed before his consecration. In the eighteenth year after his consecration, Mahinda Thera was established in this island of Sīhala. Thus, according to the royal lineage, it should be known: "He was established in this island in the two hundred and thirty-sixth year after the Parinibbāna of the Fully Enlightened Buddha."

On that day, the Jeṭṭhamūla constellation festival was held in the island of Tambapaṇṇi. The King proclaimed the festival and ordered his ministers, "Celebrate the festival." Accompanied by forty thousand men, he left the city and went to the Missaka Mountain, desiring to hunt.

Then, a deity residing on that mountain thought, "I will show the Elders to the King," and took the form of a red deer (rohitamiga), wandering nearby as if eating grass and leaves. The King saw the deer and thought, "It is not proper to shoot a deer while it is heedless," and twanged his bowstring. The deer started to flee along the path to Ambatthala. The King followed behind and climbed Ambatthala. The deer disappeared near the Elders.

Mahinda Thera, seeing the King approaching, resolved, "Let the King see only me, not the others," and said, "Tissa, Tissa, come here!" The King heard this and thought, "There is no one born on this island capable of addressing me by the name 'Tissa.' But this person, wearing torn and tattered robes, shaven-headed, wearing saffron-dyed clothes, addresses me by name. Who could this be? A human or a non-human?"

The Elder said:
"Recluses are we, O Great King, disciples of the King of Dhamma;
Out of compassion for you, we have come here from Jambudīpa."

At that time, King Devānampiyatissa and King Asoka the Righteous were friends who had never met. Due to the merit of King Devānampiyatissa, three bamboo poles the size of chariot poles appeared in a bamboo grove at the foot of Chātaka Mountain: the Creeper Pole (latāyaṭṭhi), the Flower Pole (pupphayaṭṭhi), and the Bird Pole (sakuṇayaṭṭhi). Among them, the Creeper Pole was silver-colored, and the creeper appearing as if decorating it looked golden. On the Flower Pole, flowers of blue, yellow, red, white, and black colors appeared with well-defined stalks, petals, and filaments. On the Bird Pole, various birds such as swans, cocks, and jīvajīvaka birds, and various four-footed animals appeared as if they were alive. This is also stated in the Dīpavaṃsa:
57:
“In these Three Jewels and in the noble Dispensation of the Buddha, may you also clear your mind and seek refuge with faith” (King Asoka sent this message).

## That king had been consecrated for one month on that day with the regalia sent by King Asoka.

The king had been consecrated on the full moon day of Visākhā. Recalling the news of the Dispensation he had recently heard, upon hearing the Thera's words, “Great King, we are recluses, disciples of the King of Dhamma,” he thought, “The noble ones have arrived.” At that very moment, he laid aside his weapon and sat down in one place, engaging in pleasant conversation. Regarding this:

“The king, having laid aside his weapon, sat down to one side. Having sat down, the king rejoiced, speaking many words connected with the goal,” the ancient teachers said.

While he was engaged in pleasant conversation, those forty thousand men arrived and surrounded him. Then the Thera showed the other six persons as well. When the king saw them, he asked, “When did these people arrive?” “Great King, they arrived together with me,” the Thera replied. “Are there other such recluses in Jambudīpa now?” the king asked. “Great King, there are. Now Jambudīpa is glowing with saffron robes and is wafting with the breeze of the Arahants. In that Jambudīpa:

There are many disciples of the Buddha who are possessors of the three knowledges, attained to psychic power, skilled in knowing the minds of others, and are canker-waned Arahants,” the Thera replied.

“Venerable Sir, by what means did you come?” the king asked. “Great King, neither by water nor by land,” the Thera replied. The king realized, “The noble ones must have come through the air.” The Thera, wishing to test whether the king possessed sharp wisdom, asked a question concerning a nearby mango tree: “Great King, what is the name of this tree?” “Venerable Sir, it is a mango tree.” “Great King, setting aside this mango tree, are there other mango trees?” “Venerable Sir, there are many other mango trees.” “Great King, setting aside this mango tree and those other mango trees, are there other trees?” “Venerable Sir, there are, but those trees are not mango trees.” “Setting aside the other mango trees and the trees that are not mangoes, is there any other tree?” “Venerable Sir, there is only this mango tree.” “Great King, excellent! You are wise. Great King, do you have relatives?” “Venerable Sir, there are many people.” “Great King, setting aside those relatives, are there others who are not relatives?” “Venerable Sir, those who are not relatives are more numerous than the relatives.” “Setting aside your relatives and those who are not relatives, is there anyone else?...”
58:
“Great King,” (the Thera asked). “I myself am the one who is not a relative,” the king replied. Then the Thera, thinking, “The king is wise; he will be able to understand the Dhamma,” preached the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta. At the end of the discourse, the king, along with forty thousand beings, was established in the Three Refuges. At that very moment, a meal (rice) was brought to the king. Even while listening to the Sutta, the king already knew, “It is not proper for these monks to eat at this time.” However, thinking, “It is not right to eat without asking,” he asked, “Venerable Sirs, will you take your meal?” “Great King, it is not proper for us to eat at this time,” the Thera replied. “Venerable Sir, at what time is it proper?” he asked. “Great King, it is proper to eat from dawn until noon,” the Thera replied. “Venerable Sir, let us go to the city,” the king requested. “Great King, it is not yet suitable; we will stay right here,” the Thera replied. “Venerable Sirs, if you are to remain here, let this boy come along,” the king requested again. “Great King, this boy has attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala) and has well understood the Dispensation; he is waiting for novice ordination. I shall ordain him now,” the Thera replied. The king said, “Venerable Sir, if that is so, I shall send a chariot tomorrow. Please come by that chariot,” and after paying homage, he departed.

Shortly after the king had left, the Thera called Sumaṇa Sāmaṇera and said, “Sumaṇa, come, announce the time for hearing the Dhamma.” “Venerable Sir, how far an area should I make the announcement heard?” he asked. “Announce it so that the whole of Tambapaṇṇidīpa hears it,” the Thera replied. “Very well, Venerable Sir,” the Sāmaṇera replied. He entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for supernormal knowledge, and upon emerging, he made a resolution with a concentrated mind: “Let the people within Tambapaṇṇidīpa hear!” and announced the time for hearing the Dhamma three times, making it heard throughout the whole of Tambapaṇṇidīpa. Hearing that sound, the king sent a messenger to the Theras to ask, “Venerable Sirs, is there any danger?” “There is no danger to us. We had the time for hearing the Dhamma announced because we wish to preach the words of the Buddha,” the Thera replied. Hearing the Sāmaṇera's announcement, the earth-bound deities passed the sound along. In this manner, the sound spread as far as the Brahma realm. Because of that sound, a great assembly of deities and Brahmas took place. Seeing the great assembly of deities, the Thera preached the Samacitta Sutta. At the end of the discourse, countless deities attained the realization of the Dhamma. Many Nāgas and Garuḍas were also established in the Three Refuges. Just as there was an assembly of deities when the Venerable Sāriputta preached this Sutta, a similar one occurred for the Venerable Mahinda. Then, when that night had passed, the king...
59:
The King sent a chariot for the Elders. The charioteer parked the chariot in a suitable place and informed the Elders, "Venerable sirs, the chariot has arrived; please mount it, let us go." The Elders replied, "We shall not mount the chariot; you go ahead, we will come later." Having said this, they rose into the air and descended at the site where the Pathamaka Cetiya stands, to the east of the city of Anurādhapura. Because the Cetiya was built at the very spot where the Elders first descended, it is called the "Pathamaka Cetiya."

After sending the charioteer, the King ordered his ministers, "Prepare a pavilion within the palace grounds." Immediately, all the ministers, filled with joy, prepared an exceedingly beautiful pavilion. Again, the King thought, "Yesterday, while the Elder was preaching the Sīlakkhandha, he said, 'High and luxurious seats are not allowable.' Will the venerable ones sit on the seats, or will they not?" While the King was thus reflecting, the charioteer reached the city gate. There, he saw the Elders, who had arrived before him, fastening their waistbands and donning their robes. Seeing them, he was filled with great faith, went to the King, and reported, "Great King, the Elders have arrived." The King asked, "Did they come by chariot?" "They did not come by chariot, O King; though they set out after me, they arrived before me and are standing at the eastern gate." Hearing that they did not even use the chariot, the King thought, "Now the venerable ones will not accept high and luxurious seats," and said, "Friends, if that is so, prepare seats for the Elders in the form of floor-coverings on the ground," and he went out to meet them. The ministers spread coarse mats on the ground and covered them with ornate rugs such as carpets. The soothsayers, seeing this sign, prophesied, "Now these people have taken possession of the earth; they will be the masters of the island of Tambapaṇṇi."

The King also went and paid homage to the Elders, took the alms-bowl from the hand of the Elder Mahinda, and with great honor and offerings, led the Elders into the city and into the palace. Seeing the arrangement of the seats, the Elder thought, "Our Sāsana will be established throughout the entire island of Laṅkā, spreading like the earth and remaining unshakable," and he sat down. The King personally served and satisfied the Elders with choice food and delicacies, and after they had finished, he invited five hundred women, headed by Queen Anulā, saying, "Let them pay homage and make offerings to the Elders," and then he sat down in a suitable place. At the conclusion of the meal, the Elder, raining down the rain of the Jewel of Dhamma upon the King and his retinue...
60:
...preached the Petavatthu, the Vimānavatthu, and the Saccasaṃyutta. Having heard the Elder's Dhamma teaching, those five hundred women also realized the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

The people who had seen the Elders at Missaka Mountain the previous day also spoke of the Elders' virtues in various places. Hearing those words, a great multitude of people gathered in the palace courtyard and made a great noise. The King asked, "What is this noise?" They replied, "Great King, the citizens are crying out, 'We do not get the chance to see the Elders!'" The King thought, "If they enter here into the palace, there will not be enough space," and said, "Friends, go, prepare the elephant stable, sprinkle sand, scatter flowers of five colors, hang cloth canopies, and arrange seats for the Elders at the place of the state elephant." The ministers did as the King commanded. The Elder went there, sat down, and preached the Devadūta Sutta. At the end of the discourse, a thousand beings were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. Then, thinking, "The elephant stable is too cramped," they prepared seats in the Nandana Grove at the southern gate. The Elder sat there and preached the Āsīvisopama Sutta. Having heard that teaching as well, a thousand beings attained the Fruit of Stream-entry.

Thus, on the second day from their arrival, two thousand five hundred beings attained the realization of the Dhamma. While the Elder was exchanging pleasantries with the noblewomen, daughters-in-law, and young maidens of noble families who had come to the Nandana Grove, evening arrived. Noting the time, the Elder rose and said, "Now let us return to Missaka Mountain." The ministers asked, "Venerable sirs, where are you going?" "We are going to our place of residence," he replied. After informing the King, the ministers, with the King's permission, said, "Venerable sir, it is no longer the time to go there; let this Nandana Grove itself be the dwelling place for the venerable ones." "It is not yet suitable; we shall go," he said. Again, conveying the King's words, they said, "Venerable sir, the King says, 'This grove named Mahāmeghavana belongs to my father; it is neither too far from nor too near the city, and is easy to travel to and from. Let the Elders stay here.'" The Elders then stayed in the Meghavana Grove.

When the night had passed, the King went to the Elder in the morning, asked if he had slept comfortably, and then inquired, "Venerable sir, is a park (ārāma) allowable for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus?" The Elder replied, "It is allowable, Great King," and cited this discourse: "Bhikkhus, I allow a park." The King, being delighted, took a golden pitcher, poured water over the Elder's hand, and donated the Mahāmeghavana Grove.
61:
Simultaneously with the pouring of the water, the earth trembled. This was the first earthquake in the Mahāvihāra. The King, being frightened, asked the Elder, "Venerable Sir, why does the earth tremble?" "Do not be afraid, Great King; the Dispensation of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) will be established on this island, and this will be the site of the first monastery (vihara). This is the omen of that event," he replied. The King was exceedingly pleased. On the following day, the Elder, having taken his meal in the royal palace itself, preached the Anamataggiya Suttas in the Nandanavana garden. On the next day, he preached the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta. In this manner, he preached for seven days. At the conclusion of the preaching, eighty-five hundred beings attained the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya). From that time onwards, because the Nandanavana garden was the place where the light of the Dispensation appeared, it received the name "Jotivana". On the seventh day, the Elders, having preached the Appamāda Sutta to the King in the inner palace, departed for Cetiyagiri mountain itself.

Then the King asked his ministers, "The Elder has exhorted us with a stern exhortation; has he departed?" The ministers replied, "Great King, the Elder came of his own accord without being invited by Your Majesty; therefore, his departure might also occur without asking permission." Then the King, having mounted his chariot and taking two queens with him, went to Cetiyagiri mountain with great royal majesty. Upon arrival, he had the queens stay aside at one place and approached the Elders himself, appearing very exhausted. Then the Elder asked the King, "Great King, why have you come thus exhausted?" "Venerable Sir, I have come to know whether you, having given me a stern exhortation, now wish to depart," he replied. "Great King, we do not wish to depart; however, Great King, this is the time for the commencement of the Rains Retreat (vassūpanāyika). At such a time, a monk ought to know the place for the Rains Retreat," he said. On that very day, a minister named Ariṭṭha, standing near the King together with fifty-five elder and younger brothers, said, "Great King, I wish to ordain in the presence of the Elders." "Very well, friend, do ordain," the King permitted and entrusted him to the Elder. The Elder ordained him on that very day. All of them attained Arahantship at the very end of the shaving of their hair.

The King also, at that very moment, had the courtyard of the stupa enclosed with a thorn fence, and having started the work on sixty-two caves, returned to the city. Those Elders, having inspired faith in the royal family crowded with the ten brothers and exhorting the multitude, entered the Rains Retreat at Cetiyagiri mountain. At that time, those who first entered the Rains Retreat at Cetiyagiri mountain...
62:
...there were sixty-two Arahants (at that Cetiyagiri mountain). Then, the Venerable Mahā Mahinda, having completed the Rains Retreat and performed the Great Invitation (Mahāpavarāṇā), spoke thus to the King on the Uposatha day of the full moon of Kattika: "Great King, it has been a long time since we have seen the Fully Enlightened One; we have lived as if without a refuge. We wish to go to the island of Jambudīpa." The King said, "Venerable Sir, I support you with the four requisites, and this multitude of people, depending on you, has been established in the Three Refuges. Why are you weary?" "Great King, it has been a long time since we have seen the Fully Enlightened One; there is no place (stupa) to perform the acts of salutation, rising to welcome, saluting with joined palms, and paying respect. Therefore, we are weary." "Venerable Sir, did you not say that the Fully Enlightened One has attained Parinibbāna?" he asked. "Great King, although he has attained Parinibbāna, his bodily relics still remain," he replied. "Venerable Sir, I understand that you desire the establishment of a stupa. Venerable Sir, I shall build a stupa; now, please select a site. However, Venerable Sir, from where shall we obtain the relics?" he asked. "Great King, consult with Sumana," he said.

The King, saying "Very well, Venerable Sir," approached Sumana (the novice) and asked, "Venerable Sir, from where shall we now obtain the relics?" Sumana said, "Great King, being free from anxiety, have the streets cleaned, decorated with banners, flags, and full jars, and together with your retinue, undertake the Uposatha vows. Having all kinds of musical instruments played, have the state elephant adorned with all ornaments, and having the white royal umbrella raised over the elephant, go towards the Mahānāgavana garden in the evening. Certainly, you will obtain the relics in that place." The King agreed, saying "Very well." The Elders returned to Cetiyagiri mountain itself. There, the Venerable Mahinda Thera said to Sumana Sāmaṇera: "Sāmaṇera, go to the island of Jambudīpa, approach your grandfather, the Righteous King Asoka, and speak in my name thus: 'Great King, your friend King Devānampiyatissa, having faith in the Buddha's Dispensation, wishes to establish a stupa. It is heard that there are relics in your hands; please give those relics to me.' Having taken those relics, approach Sakka, the King of Devas, and speak thus: 'Great King, it is heard that there are two relics in your hands—the right tooth relic and the right collarbone relic. Of those two, you yourself worship the right tooth relic, but give the right collarbone relic to me.' And speak to him thus: 'Great King, why do you neglect us after sending us to the island of Tambapaṇṇi?'"

Sumana, saying "Very well, Venerable Sir," accepted the Elder's words, and at that very moment, taking his bowl and robes, he rose into the air and descended at the gate of the city of Pāṭaliputta...
63:
Venerable Sumana went to the King and reported the matter. The King, being delighted, took the bowl from the novice's hand, perfumed it with scents, filled it with relics resembling excellent pearls, and gave it back. Sumana took those relics and approached Sakka, the King of the Devas. Upon seeing the novice, Sakka asked, "Venerable Sumana, why are you wandering about?" Sumana replied, "Great King, why are you being negligent after sending us to the island of Tambapaṇṇi?" Sakka said, "Venerable sir, I am not negligent. Tell me, what should I do?" Sumana said, "It is heard that you have two relics in your hand—the right tooth relic and the right collarbone relic. Of these, you should worship the right tooth relic, but give the right collarbone relic to me." Sakka, the Lord of Devas, agreed, saying, "Very well, venerable sir," and opened the gem stupa which was one league in size, took out the right collarbone relic, and gave it to Sumana. Sumana took the relic and stayed at Cetiyagiri mountain.

Then, all those great Arahants, headed by Venerable Mahinda, having properly enshrined the relics given by King Dhammāsoka at Cetiyagiri, took the right collarbone relic and went to the Mahānāgavana park at the time when the shadows were lengthening in the afternoon. The King also, having performed offerings as instructed by Sumana, mounted the shoulders of his noble elephant and, personally holding a white umbrella over the state elephant, arrived at the Mahānāgavana park. Then the King thought: "If this is truly a relic of the Fully Enlightened Buddha, may the white umbrella move aside on its own, may the state elephant kneel on the ground, and may the relic casket rest upon my head." Simultaneously with the King's thought, the umbrella moved aside, the elephant knelt, and the relic casket rested on the King's head. The King, filled with supreme joy and rapture as if his body were sprinkled with nectar, asked, "Venerable sirs, what shall I do with the relic?" They replied, "Great King, for now, place it on the elephant's frontal globe." The King took the relic casket and placed it on the elephant's frontal globe. The delighted elephant trumpeted like a crane. A great cloud arose and a shower of lilies (Pokkhara-vassa) fell. A great earthquake occurred, extending to the water's edge. Devas and humans rejoiced, saying, "The relic of the Fully Enlightened Buddha will now be established even in this remote land." Thus, generating joy in devas and humans through the glory of its miraculous power:

On the full moon day of Kattika, the Great Hero (the collarbone relic) came here from the world of the devas and rested upon the elephant's frontal globe.

Then that noble elephant, surrounded by many musicians and being honored with exceptionally grand offerings, turned to face the west, moved backward, went toward the east gate of the city, and entered the city directly through the east gate. While the citizens were making grand offerings, [he went] through the south gate...
64:
The elephant, moving backward, went as far as the east gate of the city, entered the city through the east gate, and while receiving grand offerings from all the citizens, exited through the south gate. He went to a place called Mahejavatthu to the west of Thūpārāma and then turned back to face Thūpārāma once again. At that time, Thūpārāma was the site where the personal requisites (paribhoga) of the three previous Fully Enlightened Buddhas had been enshrined as stupas.

In the past, this island was named Ojadīpa, the king was named Abhaya, the city was named Abhayapura, the Cetiyagiri mountain was named Devakūṭa, and Thūpārāma was named Paṭiyārāma. At that time, the Blessed Kakusandha appeared in the world. His disciple, the Elder Mahādeva, stayed at Devakūṭa with a thousand monks, just as the Elder Mahinda stayed at Cetiyagiri. At that time, the beings in Ojadīpa were perishing from a severe fever. When the Blessed Kakusandha surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye, he saw those beings perishing. Seeing this, he came surrounded by forty thousand monks. By the power of the Buddha, the fever was immediately pacified.
